messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leo is a 49-year-old fashion designer, a man whose professional life is built on precision, foresight, and the ability to envision a finished garment from a bolt of fabric. He came to therapy after his wife, Mira, was diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer two years ago. The trauma was not his own body, but the sight of hers—the moment in the oncologist’s office when the word “malignant” landed in the room and he watched her face go slack. That moment is burned into him, but in fragments: the fluorescent hum of the lights, the doctor’s pen tapping the edge of a clipboard, and then nothing—a blank space where the next few minutes should be. Some parts are excruciatingly clear, like the way Mira’s hand tightened on his arm, while others, like the drive home, are a complete void. This partial clarity haunts him because he feels he should remember everything, and the gaps feel like a betrayal, a failure to bear witness.

The memory of that diagnosis, when it surfaces, is not a calm recollection but a wave of overwhelming emotion that forces him to stop whatever he is doing. He will be at his drafting table, sketching a new line of evening wear, and the smell of a particular hand sanitizer—the one from the clinic—will flood his senses. He is then derailed, his heart pounding, his breath shallow, and he has to put down his pencil and walk away. The physical reactivity is immediate and uncontrollable, leaving him feeling raw and exposed. In the wake of these episodes, he is consumed by a crushing sense of guilt. He replays the moment he thinks he hesitated before asking the doctor a follow-up question, or the time he got irritated with Mira for forgetting to take a supplement. He is certain his inadequacy as a husband contributed to her suffering, and this guilt makes the memory even more potent and painful the next time it intrudes.

Because the memory is so overwhelming, Leo has developed a rigid set of strategies to contain it. He tries hard not to think about the trauma at all, a form of mental suppression that is exhausting. He keeps his mind occupied all the time, filling every waking moment with work, podcasts, or complex crossword puzzles. He has also stopped making any plans for the future. When his colleagues ask about the spring collection or a vacation with Mira, he deflects with a vague comment about “taking it day by day.” This avoidance of future plans is a direct consequence of his memory: every time he tries to imagine a happy event—a holiday, a retirement party—the image is instantly replaced by the blank, fluorescent-lit room of the diagnosis. Planning feels like tempting fate, an invitation for the other shoe to drop.

The threat he feels is constant and diffuse. He experiences strong negative feelings—fear, anger, and a deep, corrosive shame that he cannot protect Mira. He has trouble falling asleep because his mind races with worst-case scenarios; he lies awake monitoring his own heartbeat, listening for any sound from her side of the bed. This hypervigilance, in turn, feeds back into his memory. When he is already on edge, the intrusive memories feel more vivid and more terrifying, creating a self-reinforcing loop where his anxiety primes him for a flashback, and the flashback ratchets his anxiety even higher. He will catch himself scanning the faces of strangers at the grocery store, looking for signs of illness, a habit that leaves him drained.

His suppression and mental distraction, the very strategies meant to control the memory, paradoxically strengthen it. The more he tries to push the memory away during the day, the more it erupts in fragmented, guilt-laden intrusions at night or in quiet moments. His mind, starved of processing time, seems to fight back. The only consequence of this cycle that Leo can name is his growing distance from Mira. He is so busy keeping his mind occupied and avoiding all reminders—including conversations about the future—that he has become a silent, shadowy presence in their home. He is present but unreachable, a husband who has turned his back on the very thing he is most afraid of losing.

He finally sought help not for himself, but because Mira told him she felt like she was going through her cancer treatment alone. What frightens him most is not the memory of the diagnosis, but the possibility that his fear of the past is destroying his chance at a future with the woman he loves.
